ingredients.item: large shrimp , shell on, deveined, or shell-off if the table prefers peeling-free eating
Steamed rice , oi muchim , lettuce ssam

instructions.heading: Step 1
instructions.action: Dry shrimp onto a hot grate or pan in a single layer, two minutes undisturbed. If shell-on, they will char lightly at the edges; that char is the flavor and the table peels it off later.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: the shells blush pink-white and the undersides show grill marks through the shell; shell-off shrimp turn opaque at the bottom edge and roll loosely on the grate.

instructions.heading: Step 2
instructions.action: Flip once, one minute more — the shrimp are nearly done now. Brush the glaze on the up faces, wait 30 seconds, flip, brush the second faces, 30 seconds, off the fire.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: the glaze sets glossy and brick-toned in that final minute. If it blackens, the fire was past the glaze's tolerance — the shrimp are still good; note the notch down for the next batch.

instructions.heading: Step 3
instructions.action: Sesame and scallion over, platter, straight to the table — shrimp wait for nobody.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: eating test: sweet-heat glaze on the first chew, then the shrimp's own snap and sweetness — the glaze should coat, not bury. One test shrimp that tastes only of gochujang means the coating ran thick; a thin brush-stroke is the whole technique.

storageNotes: Raw shrimp in the glaze hold 30 minutes, no more — the salt starts curing. Cooked, 2 days; the shells make a quick stock for the next day's jjigae.
Variations: the soy-garlic fork (#SF02) for the clean lane; the same glaze on scallops (#SF03's cousin); cho-gochujang (#SA03) served beside as the dip instead of brushed.
